You are starting from zero. German has formal and informal ways to say 'you'. Start with informal du.
For 'I am', say ich bin. For 'my name is', say ich heiße. A normal German statement usually puts the conjugated verb second.
Introduce yourself and ask another person’s name.
To say where you come from, use ich komme aus. To say where you live, use ich wohne in.
German verbs change with the subject: ich komme, du kommst. In a statement, the verb stays in second position.
Ich komme aus den USA. Ich wohne in Virginia.
I come from the USA. I live in Virginia.
Say where you come from and where you live.
You can ask questions by starting with a question word or by putting the verb first for a yes/no question.
Question words: wer (who), was (what), wo (where), wie (how). Yes/no question: Sprichst du Deutsch?
Sprichst du Deutsch? Ja, ein bisschen.
Do you speak German? Yes, a little.
Ask three simple questions and answer them.
Start with numbers 1–10. Learn them by saying them in sequence, then out of sequence.
For clock time, Wie spät ist es? means 'What time is it?' Es ist drei Uhr = It's three o'clock.
Say your age and tell the time.
German nouns have grammatical genders. Learn each noun with its article: der, die, or das.
Ich möchte ... means 'I would like ...'. Use it to make polite orders. With masculine accusative nouns, der becomes den.
Order a drink and something to eat.
Useful restaurant language consists of short, reusable chunks. Practice saying each without translating word-by-word.
Ich hätte gern ... is another polite way to order. Die Rechnung, bitte asks for the bill.
Order food, request the bill, and thank the server.
Direction words are most useful as complete questions. Practice with imaginary locations.
Wo ist ...? asks where something is. Links, rechts and geradeaus mean left, right and straight ahead.
Ask where the train station is and understand basic directions.
Travel language builds on directions. Listen for platform, departure and arrival.
German separable verbs split in main clauses: Der Zug fährt um acht Uhr ab. The prefix ab goes to the end.
Ask about train departure and buy a ticket.
Use simple sentences to talk about people. German nouns are capitalized.
Mein and meine both mean 'my'. Use mein before masculine/neuter singular nouns and meine before feminine/plural nouns in the nominative.
Describe your family or two people you know.
Talk about what you do every day using present-tense verbs.
In ordinary statements the conjugated verb comes second: Ich arbeite heute. Heute arbeite ich. Both mean 'I work today'.
German separable verbs let you describe daily routines. Learn the entire sentence.
Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf: the prefix auf moves to the end in a normal main clause.
Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
I get up at seven o'clock.
Describe waking up, working, eating, and sleeping.
I get up at seven o'clock.
Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
What you can and must do
Modal verbs express ability, obligation, and wishes.
Ich kann = I can; ich muss = I must; ich will = I want. The second verb stays in infinitive at the end: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.
Ich kann ein bisschen Deutsch sprechen.
I can speak a little German.
Explain what you can, must, and want to do.
I can speak a little German.
Ich kann ein bisschen Deutsch sprechen.
German often uses the Perfekt tense in conversation: a helping verb plus past participle.
Ich habe gelernt = I learned. Ich bin gefahren = I traveled by vehicle. Motion/change verbs often use sein.
Tell someone three things you did yesterday.
Connect ideas instead of using only short sentences.
Weil means because and pushes the conjugated verb to the end: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich reisen möchte.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich reisen möchte.
I learn German because I want to travel.
Explain why you're learning German and describe your plans.
I learn German because I want to travel.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich reisen möchte.
Polite requests and explanations help you handle real conversations.
Könnten Sie ...? is a polite request. Ich denke, dass ... introduces an opinion; the conjugated verb moves to the end of the dass clause.
Explain a problem, ask for help, and express an opinion.
